source.title: The Joint Effect of Quantization and Sampling Temperature on LLM Safety Alignment: A Factorial Analysis

page_placements.theme: Compression, pruning and noise have conditional safety effects

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no garbling or cut-off is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether an inference-time decoding change—sampling temperature—alters harmful-response rates, and reports results for an adversarial-suffix benchmark. These are conceptual tests of parts of V4, not tests of the original fine-tuning or token-position methods.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates temperature and quantization, not fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization, or safety-deepening training. It includes GCG-AdvBench results, but does not report a matched intervention that adds or removes suffixes. DFR is a decision-instability measure, not a harmful-completion rate; those results are recorded as findings outside the listed versions.
record.test_reason: A deployment study of quantization and temperature. It bears on V4 in two ways: a matched suffix-versus-no-suffix comparison (GCG-AdvBench is AdvBench plus a GCG suffix) and a temperature sweep of 0–1.0. Shallow alignment is not its aim, so this is a new setting (T3) rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that standard quantization is approximately safety-neutral except for SmolLM3-3B, that temperature mainly increases decision instability rather than pooled ASR, and that the two factors are sub-additive rather than compounding. They recommend multi-sample stability metrics across multiple benchmarks, since AdvBench alone understates risk.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies post-training quantization and inference temperature; it does not fine-tune models on harmful or benign examples or measure response-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Temperature affects DFR more strongly than pooled ASR; results also vary by model and benchmark. The paper reports judge disagreement, especially on harder benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: Decision flip rate at FP16/T=1.0 reaches 41.9% (Mistral-7B) and 38.6% (SmolLM3-3B), about 15% for Qwen, and ≤5.6% for Llama.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Higher sampling temperature increases within-prompt variability of safety decisions even when majority-vote ASR is flat.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard quantization changes pooled ASR by ≤1.6 pp for 7 of 8 models; INT4 raises SmolLM3-3B from 34.5% to 44.1%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard PTQ is roughly safety-neutral, with exceptions in weakly aligned models.

fits_no_version.finding: Many-shot framing (ManyHarm) gives 80–100% ASR in models with 0% on AdvBench (Granite, Qwen3-4B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Many-shot in-context harmful framing defeats refusal in models that refuse direct requests.

record.problems: The study uses 2B–8B models and static prompt sets; the authors note that adaptive jailbreaks may differ. Safety judges are imperfect and disagree, particularly on harder benchmarks. Two INT4 checkpoints required a separate re-quantization run after the default export collapsed.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result rows were left out.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant opening; per-model optimized suffixes; decoding changes other than temperature ≤1.0 (top-p, top-k, best-of-n sampling). ASR uses a majority vote over 5 samples, so 'any sample harmful' sampling attacks are not measured.
Per-token KL by response position: not studied.
Parameter localization of safety: not studied. Quantization perturbs all weights and is not a localization test.

missing.what: Mistral-7B FP16 AdvBench and GCG-AdvBench ASR rise +14.5 pp from T=0 to T=1.0, while ManyHarm falls −26 pp
Per-benchmark AdvBench and GCG-AdvBench ASR vs temperature for the other seven models (figure only, values not stated)
Per-benchmark ManyHarm ASR at FP16/T=0 (e.g. Granite 0% AdvBench vs 100% ManyHarm), relevant as an in-context attack

record.verdict_notes: Two caveats weaken the challenges. ASR counts a prompt harmful only if most of its 5 samples are unsafe, so it understates sampling-based bypass; high DFR implies many prompts with at least one unsafe sample. The GCG suffixes appear to be fixed and transferred, not optimized against each model. Models are 2B–8B. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.

Prefilling a compliant opening and decoding changes other than temperature. The paper reports GCG-AdvBench scores but does not isolate the causal effect of adding a suffix against a matched no-suffix prompt.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives produce shallow safety behaviour.
Training to deepen safety beyond the first tokens and whether that training holds up.

relation.reason: Its own suffix comparisons and temperature sweeps measure harmful compliance and therefore bear on V4.

tranche.reason: A deployment-factor study supplies results bearing on V4 in a new setting; shallow alignment is not its primary question.

source_check.notes: All prompt sets are static; per-model suffix optimization is unstated, so the suffix result does not establish resistance to adaptive GCG. The Mistral benchmark-specific temperature result underlying l2 needs a separate row because r18 records only the pooled mean.

statements.correction: At T=0, AWQ INT4 increases pooled ASR by at most 1.6 pp or reduces it for seven of eight models. Qwen3-8B decreases by 5.9 pp under INT4 and 7.5 pp under INT8; Qwen3-4B increases by 2.7 pp under INT8; Mistral-7B decreases by 1.7 pp under INT8. SmolLM3-3B rises from 34.5% FP16 to 44.1% INT4.
statements.problem: The ≤1.6 pp claim conflates a bound on INT4 increases with an absolute bound on PTQ changes; Tables 2–3 show larger changes for several models.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The paper describes pooled ASR as largely temperature-insensitive; Mistral-7B stays near 34–35%, and SmolLM3-3B INT4 decreases rather than becoming less safe (r17–r19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: GCG-AdvBench ASR ranges from 0.0% to 28.5% and equals the corresponding AdvBench rate for every model, so the reported benchmark does not show a uniform increase attributable to the suffix (r02, r04, r06, r08, r10, r12, r14, r16).
